title: Caching and Search Stores
tagline: Redis for sub-millisecond speed, eviction policies for memory control, and inverted indexes for full-text search at scale.

sections.content:
Every production system eventually hits the same wall: the database is fast enough in development, but under real load — thousands of requests per second, data growing into hundreds of gigabytes — the query latency climbs, the CPU saturates, and users start complaining. The root cause is almost always the same: the application is reading the same data repeatedly from a storage layer that was never designed to be hammered that hard.

**Caching** is the practice of storing the results of expensive computations or slow storage lookups in a faster, closer layer so that subsequent requests get the answer without repeating the work. Done well, caching is the single highest-leverage performance improvement available to a backend engineer — it can cut p99 latency from hundreds of milliseconds to under a millisecond and reduce database load by an order of magnitude.

**Redis** (Remote Dictionary Server) is the dominant in-memory data store for caching and much more. Released in 2009 by Salvatore Sanfilippo, it stores data entirely in RAM, making reads and writes absurdly fast — typically under 0.1 milliseconds. But Redis is not a dumb key-value store: it supports rich data types (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams), built-in expiry (TTL), Lua scripting, pub/sub messaging, optional persistence to disk, and cluster mode for horizontal sharding. (Since 2024 there are two lineages — Redis and its BSD-licensed fork **Valkey** — see the licensing note below.) Understanding Redis well means understanding which data structure to reach for and which eviction policy to apply when memory is constrained.

Full-text search is a fundamentally different problem. When a user types a search query on an e-commerce site, you are not looking for rows where a single column matches exactly — you want to rank millions of product descriptions by how relevant they are to the query, handle stemming ("run" matching "running"), and do it in milliseconds. SQL `LIKE '%keyword%'` cannot do this at scale. **Elasticsearch** (and **OpenSearch**, the fork AWS created in 2021 after Elastic changed Elasticsearch's license) solves this by prebuilding an **inverted index** — a data structure that maps every token in your corpus to the list of documents containing it, enabling fast lookup with sophisticated relevance scoring via the **BM25** algorithm.

This chapter covers both worlds in depth: the mechanics and patterns of Redis caching, the eviction strategies that govern memory under pressure, the internals of inverted indexes, and the practical decisions that separate a naive cache from a resilient production system.

sections.title: The Whiteboard Menu, the Recipe Book, and the Library Card Catalog
sections.content:
Picture a high-volume restaurant. The full recipe book locked in the kitchen (the database) contains every dish ever served — authoritative, comprehensive, but slow to consult. The whiteboard by the counter (Redis) lists tonight's specials in plain sight: pre-computed answers to the most common questions. When a customer asks for today's soup, the server reads the whiteboard in an instant. If the soup isn't listed, the server walks back to the kitchen, looks up the recipe, then writes it on the whiteboard for the next customer. The whiteboard has limited space, so when it fills up, someone erases the items that have been sitting longest without anyone ordering them — that is LRU eviction.

Now imagine you run a library and a patron walks in asking for every book that mentions the phrase 'quantum entanglement'. You cannot open every book and search page by page — that would take hours. Instead, you have a **card catalog** (the inverted index) where, under the entry 'quantum', there is a list of book IDs, and under 'entanglement', another list. You intersect those two lists in seconds and hand the patron exactly the matching titles, ranked by how many times the phrase appears.

Redis is the whiteboard. Elasticsearch is the card catalog. Both serve the same master goal: answering questions faster by preparing the answer before the question is asked.

sections.title: Redis Data Types: Choosing the Right Tool
sections.content:
Redis's power comes from its rich collection of built-in data structures. Each has distinct time complexity characteristics and maps to different real-world use cases. Choosing the wrong type is a common source of both bugs and wasted memory.

**Strings** are the most fundamental type. Despite the name, they can hold any binary data up to 512 MB — serialised JSON, compressed blobs, or plain text. The `SET` / `GET` pair is O(1). Strings also support atomic integer operations: `INCR`, `DECR`, `INCRBY`. Because Redis executes commands one at a time on a single main thread (network I/O can use extra threads since 6.0, command execution cannot), `INCR` on a string key is race-condition-free — two concurrent clients cannot interleave their read-modify-write cycles. This makes strings ideal for counters, rate-limit buckets, and session tokens.

**Hashes** store a collection of field-value pairs under a single key — conceptually like a database row or a Python dict. `HSET user:1001 name Alice age 30 role admin` stores three fields atomically. `HGET user:1001 name` retrieves one field in O(1). `HGETALL` returns all fields in O(n) where n is the number of fields. Hashes are more memory-efficient than storing each field as a separate string key when a Redis object has many attributes, because Redis uses a compact `listpack` encoding internally for small hashes (called `ziplist` before Redis 7.0).

**Lists** are ordered sequences (internally a *quicklist*: a doubly linked list of compact listpack chunks) supporting O(1) push and pop from both ends: `LPUSH` / `RPUSH` to push, `LPOP` / `RPOP` to pop. `LRANGE key 0 -1` retrieves all elements in O(n). Lists are natural queues (push to right, pop from left) or stacks (push and pop from the same end). They are also used for activity feeds where you keep the N most recent items using `LTRIM`.

**Sets** store unique, unordered members with O(1) average complexity for add, remove, and membership test. The power of sets lies in set operations: `SUNION`, `SINTER`, `SDIFF` compute unions, intersections, and differences, enabling features like 'users who bought A also bought B' or 'mutual friends'.

**Sorted Sets (ZSETs)** are sets where each member has an associated floating-point **score**. Members are stored in ascending score order. `ZADD leaderboard 4200 user:1001` adds a member with score 4200. `ZRANGE leaderboard 0 9 REV WITHSCORES` (the older spelling `ZREVRANGE` still works) retrieves the top 10 in O(log n + k). Sorted sets are the correct data structure for leaderboards, priority queues, time-windowed rate limiting (score = timestamp), and any use case that needs 'give me the k members with the highest/lowest score'.

**Streams** (added in Redis 5.0) are an append-only log with consumer group support — essentially Kafka-lite built into Redis. Each entry has an auto-generated or user-specified ID and arbitrary fields. Streams support `XADD` to append, `XREAD` to read from a position, and consumer groups for distributed processing. They are ideal for event sourcing, real-time analytics, and activity logs where you need replay semantics.

sections.title: TTL and Cache Expiry: The Art of Staleness
sections.content:
Every piece of cached data has a freshness window — a period during which it is close enough to the truth to be useful. After that window, it becomes **stale**: it no longer reflects the source of truth and may mislead users or trigger incorrect business logic.

Redis manages freshness through **TTL (Time-To-Live)**: `SET user:1001 '{...}' EX 300` sets the key to expire in 300 seconds. Redis removes expired keys lazily (when they are next accessed) and periodically (a background sweep), so memory is reclaimed without a dedicated garbage collector thread.

Setting the right TTL is a judgment call that balances consistency and performance:
- **Too short** (e.g., 5 seconds): the cache barely helps — most requests are still cache misses. You get the complexity of caching without the latency benefit.
- **Too long** (e.g., 24 hours): stale data can cause real problems — a user sees an outdated price, a dashboard shows incorrect metrics, or a permission check reflects a revoked role.
- A common starting point for user-facing data is **60–300 seconds** for data that changes infrequently, and **5–30 seconds** for data that changes more often but where brief staleness is acceptable.

When staleness is not acceptable at all, you need **active invalidation**: the application explicitly deletes the Redis key whenever the underlying data changes. The combination of a modest TTL plus active invalidation (TTL as the safety net, active invalidation as the primary mechanism) is robust and widely used in production.

**Volatile vs. persistent keys**: Redis lets you mix keys with TTLs and keys without TTLs in the same instance. Keys without TTLs are 'persistent' — they survive until explicitly deleted or evicted. This allows you to use a single Redis instance as both a cache (volatile keys) and a durable store (persistent keys), though you need to configure eviction policy carefully when doing so.

sections.title: Eviction Policies: What Happens When Redis Runs Out of Memory
sections.content:
Redis is configured with a `maxmemory` limit. When that limit is reached, Redis must either refuse new writes or remove existing keys to make room. Which keys it removes is controlled by the **eviction policy** (`maxmemory-policy` in `redis.conf`).

**`noeviction`** (the default) returns an `OOM command not allowed` error when memory is full. This is appropriate only when Redis is used as a primary data store where data loss from eviction would be catastrophic — for example, a Celery task queue where losing a task means it never runs. It is almost never the right choice for a cache.

**`allkeys-lru`** evicts the **Least Recently Used** key across all keys, regardless of whether they have a TTL. This is the most common production choice for a pure cache: any key can be evicted, and Redis makes room for new data by removing what has not been used recently. The LRU approximation in Redis is probabilistic — it samples a configurable number of keys (default 5) and evicts the stalest among the sample, which is cheaper than maintaining a strict LRU list.

**`volatile-lru`** applies LRU eviction only to keys that have a TTL set. Keys without a TTL are never evicted. This is useful when Redis holds both cached data (volatile, can be evicted) and critical application data (no TTL, must survive). The risk: if no keys with a TTL are left to evict, this policy behaves like `noeviction` and writes start failing with OOM errors.

**`allkeys-lfu`** evicts the **Least Frequently Used** key. LFU tracks an approximate access count per key (with exponential decay over time). When access patterns have strong hot/cold skew — a small set of 'hot' keys are accessed millions of times while a long tail of 'cold' keys are rarely accessed — LFU keeps the hot keys in memory more reliably than LRU. LFU was added in Redis 4.0.

**`volatile-lfu`** applies LFU logic only to keys with TTLs, analogous to `volatile-lru`.

**`allkeys-random`** / **`volatile-random`** evict a random key (from all keys, or only from keys with a TTL). Rarely the best choice, but the cheapest to run and fine when access is uniformly random.

**`volatile-ttl`** evicts the key with the shortest remaining TTL — the key that was about to expire anyway. This makes intuitive sense as a 'help the cache clean itself' policy, though in practice `allkeys-lru` is more effective for general caching.

sections.title: Persistence, Threading, and Durability
sections.content:
Redis keeps the dataset in RAM, but it can persist it to disk in two ways:

- **RDB snapshots**: a forked child process writes a point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset (on a schedule such as `save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000`, or on `BGSAVE`). Compact and fast to restart from, but a crash loses everything written since the last snapshot — and the fork can briefly double memory use on a write-heavy instance.
- **AOF (append-only file)**: every write command is appended to a log. With `appendfsync everysec` (the usual setting) Redis fsyncs once per second, so a crash loses about a second of writes; `always` fsyncs on every write (much slower); `no` leaves flushing to the OS. The AOF is periodically rewritten (compacted) in the background.

Many deployments enable both, and pure caches often disable persistence entirely. Replication is **asynchronous**: the primary acknowledges a write before replicas have it, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes. `WAIT numreplicas timeout` narrows that window but does not make Redis a strongly consistent store.

**Threading**: commands execute on a single main thread. That is why every command — and every `MULTI`/`EXEC` block or Lua script — is atomic, and also why one slow command (`KEYS *`, `SMEMBERS` on a huge set, a long Lua script) stalls *every* client. Since Redis 6.0, optional **I/O threads** (`io-threads`) read requests and write responses in parallel, and background threads handle tasks such as lazy freeing (`UNLINK`) — but command execution stays single-threaded. To scale throughput, add shards (Redis Cluster splits keys into 16,384 hash slots across primaries) rather than buying a bigger machine.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The cache-aside pattern in `getUserProfile` is the bread-and-butter of Redis usage; it also caches "user not found" for 30 seconds so repeated lookups of a missing ID cannot hammer the database. Redis stores strings, so objects must be serialised. `MULTI`/`EXEC` makes the INCR+EXPIRE and HSET+EXPIRE pairs atomic. `SET NX EX` acquires a lock in one atomic command (the old `SETNX` + `EXPIRE` pair had a crash window), and the random token matters on release: if your lock expired and someone else acquired it, a plain `DEL` would delete *their* lock — the Lua script deletes only when the value is still yours.

sections.title: Cache Patterns: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Behind
sections.content:
The way an application interacts with the cache on reads and writes defines the **cache pattern**. Each pattern has a different consistency/performance trade-off.

**Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)** is the most prevalent pattern. The application is the mediator: on a read, it checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads the database and writes the result to the cache. On a write, it updates the database and then either deletes the cache key (invalidation) or updates it directly. The advantages are simplicity and resilience — if Redis goes down, the application still works (just slower). The disadvantage is that the first request after a cache miss (or after startup) is slow, and there is a brief window of stale data between a database write and cache invalidation.

**Write-Through** updates the cache and the database synchronously on every write. The application writes to the cache, and the cache (or a middleware layer) immediately propagates the write to the database before acknowledging success. This keeps the cache perfectly consistent with the database at all times. The cost is increased write latency (you wait for both layers) and wasted cache space for data that is written once but never read.

**Write-Behind (Write-Back)** acknowledges the write after updating the cache only, then asynchronously flushes the change to the database in batches. This is very fast for write-heavy workloads — the database sees fewer, larger writes. The critical risk: if the cache node crashes before the async flush, you lose the uncommitted writes. Write-behind is used in embedded systems, databases (their own internal buffer pools use this pattern), and applications where write throughput is paramount and brief data loss is acceptable.

**Read-Through** is a variant of cache-aside where the cache itself (rather than the application) is responsible for loading data from the database on a miss. The application only ever talks to the cache layer. This simplifies application code but requires a cache that supports a 'loader' function — Redis does not do this natively. In-process libraries (Caffeine's `LoadingCache` in Java, ORM second-level caches) and managed services such as Amazon DAX for DynamoDB provide it.

In practice, most web applications use **cache-aside for reads** combined with **TTL + active invalidation for writes**: the TTL acts as the safety net (stale data never lives forever), and the invalidation (delete the key on write) provides near-immediate consistency.

sections.title: Cache Stampede and How to Prevent It
sections.content:
One of the most dangerous failure modes in caching is the **cache stampede** (also called 'thundering herd'). Here is the scenario: a popular key — say, the homepage product listing for an e-commerce site — expires simultaneously in Redis. In the window between expiry and the first successful repopulation, hundreds or thousands of concurrent requests all find the cache empty and all proceed to query the database at the same time. The database, which was handling maybe 10 queries per second from Redis misses under normal load, suddenly gets slammed with 500 queries in the same second. It can crash or degrade severely, causing a cascading failure.

The root cause is a **thundering herd**: many actors waking up simultaneously to do the same expensive work. There are several mitigation strategies:

**Mutex locking**: When a request finds the cache empty, it tries to acquire a Redis distributed lock (via `SET NX EX`). Only the request that acquires the lock fetches from the database and repopulates the cache. Other requests either wait briefly and retry (spinning), or return a stale value if one is available. This eliminates parallel database fetches but introduces a brief wait for the non-lock-holders.

**Probabilistic early expiration (PER)**: Instead of a hard expiry boundary, each request that reads a key near its expiry time independently decides — with some probability — to refresh it early. The formula typically involves the remaining TTL and a random draw. As the TTL approaches zero, the probability of early refresh increases. The result is that the cache gets refreshed before it expires, staggered across multiple requests, with no stampede window. This technique (often called *XFetch*) was analysed by Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein in 2015. Facebook's memcache deployment solved the same problem differently, with **leases**: on a miss, memcache hands out a lease token to one client, and other clients are told to wait briefly and retry.

**Background refresh**: The application serves the stale value immediately and asynchronously triggers a background job to refresh the cache. The user never sees a slow request; they might see data that is slightly old for one request cycle. This works well for data where brief staleness is acceptable (dashboards, analytics).

**Request coalescing and TTL jitter**: inside one process, collapse concurrent misses for the same key into a single in-flight database call (Go's `singleflight`, a shared promise in Node.js). Across keys, add random jitter to TTLs (e.g. 300 s ± 10%) so thousands of keys written at the same moment — after a deploy or cache flush — do not all expire in the same second.

**Serve stale on miss**: Cache the data indefinitely (no TTL) but store the intended expiry inside the value. When a request reads a key that is past its logical expiry, return the stale value immediately and trigger an async refresh. The first request after expiry is fast (stale data), subsequent requests get fresh data once the background fetch completes.

sections.title: Inverted Index: The Engine Behind Full-Text Search
sections.content:
A relational database is optimised for structured queries — find rows where `price < 100` and `category = 'electronics'`. These are **point or range lookups** on indexed columns, and B+ tree indexes handle them beautifully.

Full-text search is a different problem in kind. When a user searches for 'wireless mechanical keyboard', they want:
1. Every document that mentions any of those words (or related forms like 'keyboards', 'mechanically')
2. Documents ranked by **relevance** — how well do they match the query?
3. Fuzzy tolerance — typos, stemming, synonyms
4. Results in milliseconds across millions of documents

SQL `LIKE '%wireless%'` fails on all four counts: a leading wildcard disables the B+ tree index and forces a full table scan, there is no relevance ranking, and there is no stemming or fuzzy matching.

The solution is an **inverted index**. During **indexing**, every document is passed through an **analysis pipeline**:
1. **Tokenisation**: split text into tokens (words). 'Fast wireless keyboard' → ['Fast', 'wireless', 'keyboard']
2. **Lowercasing**: normalise case → ['fast', 'wireless', 'keyboard']
3. **Stemming / lemmatisation**: reduce words to their root form → ['fast', 'wireless', 'keyboard'] (here no change, but 'running' → 'run', 'keyboards' → 'keyboard')
4. **Stop word removal**: remove common words with low discriminating power → remove 'the', 'is', 'a'
5. **Synonym expansion** (optional): add related terms

The result of this pipeline is a list of **terms** (normalised tokens). The inverted index maps each term to a **posting list** — an ordered list of document IDs (and optionally: term positions, term frequency counts) where that term appears.

At **query time**, the search engine applies the same analysis pipeline to the query string, looks up each resulting term in the inverted index, and combines the posting lists — intersecting for AND queries, unioning for OR — to find matching document IDs. Lucene stores the term dictionary as a compact, sorted, prefix-compressed structure (a finite-state transducer), so finding a term costs roughly O(length of the term), followed by an O(k) walk of the posting list, where k is the number of matching documents (skip data lets AND-intersections jump ahead). For a single-term query on a corpus of 100 million documents, this might take a few milliseconds.

**Relevance scoring** is then applied to rank the matching documents. The dominant algorithm is **BM25** (Best Match 25), which extends the earlier TF-IDF formula with saturation and length normalisation:
- **Term Frequency (TF)**: how often does the query term appear in this document? More occurrences → more relevant, but with diminishing returns (saturation prevents a document from gaming the score by repeating a word 1000 times).
- **Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)**: how rare is this term across the entire corpus? A term that appears in 90% of documents ('the', 'product') carries little discriminating information; a term that appears in 0.01% of documents is highly distinctive and should be weighted more heavily.
- **Length normalisation**: shorter documents that mention a term are considered more focused on that term than long documents. A 50-word product description containing 'keyboard' is a better match than a 10,000-word review that also mentions it once.

Modern search adds **vector (semantic) search**: documents and queries are embedded as dense vectors and matched by approximate nearest-neighbour search (usually HNSW graphs), which finds 'cordless keyboard' for a 'wireless keyboard' query even with no shared terms. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and PostgreSQL's pgvector all support it, and **hybrid search** — combining BM25 and vector rankings, for example with reciprocal rank fusion — is now the common default for product search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `mappings` block defines how each field is analysed. `text` fields are tokenised and stemmed — searching 'keyboards' will match 'keyboard'. `keyword` fields are stored as-is for exact matches (used in filters and aggregations). The `bool` query combines `must` (full-text relevance) with `filter` (hard constraints like `in_stock: true` and `price <= 200`). Filters do not affect the relevance score and can be cached. Boosting belongs at query time (`name^3`); index-time `boost` in mappings is deprecated. Since client v8 the request fields go at the top level — the old `body:` wrapper was removed in v9.

sections.title: Do You Need Elasticsearch? PostgreSQL Full-Text Search
sections.content:
For a single application with up to millions or tens of millions of documents, PostgreSQL's built-in full-text search is often enough. A `tsvector` column stores each row's analysed terms, a **GIN index** (an inverted index) maps every term to the rows that contain it, and the `@@` operator matches a `tsquery`. You get stemming, stop words, field weights and ranking — plus transactional consistency with the rest of your data (no sync pipeline, no refresh delay) and one less cluster to run.

The limits are real, though: `ts_rank` is not BM25 and ignores corpus-wide term statistics, typo tolerance needs the separate `pg_trgm` extension, and faceting, relevance tuning, and horizontal scale-out are much weaker than in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch. A common path is to start in PostgreSQL and move search out when relevance or scale demands it.

sections.label: PostgreSQL FTS
sections.code:
-- Full-text search inside PostgreSQL (12+ for generated columns)
CREATE TABLE products (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name        text NOT NULL,
  description text NOT NULL,
  search      tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
                setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
                setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
              ) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search);

INSERT INTO products (name, description) VALUES
  ('Wireless Mechanical Keyboard', 'Ultra-fast wireless keyboard for gaming'),
  ('Wired Optical Mouse', 'Ergonomic mouse for office work');

-- websearch_to_tsquery accepts Google-style input: "quoted phrases", -exclude, OR
SELECT id, name, ts_rank(search, query) AS rank
FROM products, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'wireless keyboards') AS query
WHERE search @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 10;
-- 'keyboards' is stemmed to 'keyboard' -> returns the keyboard row

-- Typo tolerance needs trigrams, not tsvector
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
SELECT name, word_similarity('keybord', name) AS sim
FROM products
WHERE 'keybord' <% name          -- word-similarity match (default threshold 0.6)
ORDER BY sim DESC;
sections.explanation: The generated `search` column keeps the `tsvector` in sync automatically on every insert and update, and field weights (A for name, B for description) make title matches rank higher. The GIN index is PostgreSQL's inverted index: term → rows. `<%` uses trigram word similarity, so a misspelled query still finds "Keyboard"; add a GIN index with `gin_trgm_ops` to make it fast on large tables.

sections.title: Elasticsearch Architecture: Shards, Replicas, and the Distributed Index
sections.content:
A single Elasticsearch **index** is divided into **shards** — each shard is a self-contained Lucene index (Lucene is the Java library that implements the actual inverted index). Sharding enables horizontal scaling: a 10-shard index spreads data and query load across 10 nodes, and searches are executed in parallel across all shards with results merged on the coordinating node.

Each shard can have one or more **replicas** — identical copies on other nodes. Replicas serve two purposes: fault tolerance (if a primary shard's node fails, a replica is promoted) and read scaling (search queries can be routed to replicas, distributing read load).

Since Elasticsearch 7 a new index defaults to **1 primary shard**. The primary count is fixed at creation — changing it means the `_split`/`_shrink` APIs or a full reindex — so size it for the data: a common guideline is roughly 10–50 GB per shard. Time-based data (logs) sidesteps the problem with rollover: a new index per day or per size threshold. Set `number_of_replicas` to at least 1 in production.

The **refresh interval** is critical for performance understanding. By default, Elasticsearch makes new documents searchable every **1 second** (the 'near real-time' guarantee). During a refresh, the in-memory indexing buffer is written as a new Lucene segment into the filesystem cache — searchable, but not yet fsynced. Durability comes from the **translog**, a per-shard write-ahead log that by default is fsynced before each index request is acknowledged; a periodic **flush** fsyncs the segments and trims the translog, and background merges combine small segments. This means there is always up to a 1-second delay between indexing a document and it being searchable — important to account for in real-time use cases. For batch indexing, setting `refresh_interval: -1` during the bulk load and then re-enabling it afterward dramatically improves throughput.

**Redis vs. Memcached**: Memcached (2003) is an older, simpler alternative to Redis. It supports only string key-value pairs and offers no persistence, pub/sub, scripting, or rich data types. Redis supersedes Memcached for almost all use cases. Memcached is multi-threaded and can be faster per node for simple string lookups (Redis executes commands on one thread), but the operational simplicity of maintaining one caching system and the power of Redis's data types make it the dominant choice. As of Redis 6.0, Redis also supports multi-threaded I/O (not command execution), narrowing the throughput gap.

**Elasticsearch vs. dedicated databases**: Elasticsearch excels at full-text search and log analytics but is not a replacement for a relational database. It does not support ACID transactions, its update model is internally delete-and-reinsert (making partial updates expensive at scale), and it requires substantial operational overhead (JVM tuning, shard management, cluster monitoring). Use Elasticsearch for what it does uniquely well — full-text search and aggregations over large document sets — and keep your source of truth in a relational or document database.

**Licensing and forks (as of 2026)**: In March 2024 Redis Ltd. moved Redis (from 7.4) off the BSD license to source-available terms (RSALv2 / SSPLv1). The Linux Foundation responded with **Valkey**, a BSD-licensed fork of Redis 7.2.4 backed by AWS, Google, Oracle and others; cloud providers now offer managed Valkey (for example Amazon ElastiCache and Google Memorystore). In 2025 Redis 8 added **AGPLv3** as an option, making Redis OSI open source again. For everyday commands, clients and the RESP protocol the two remain compatible, though newer features are diverging. Search went through the same arc earlier: Elastic moved Elasticsearch from Apache 2.0 to SSPL/Elastic License in 2021, AWS forked the last Apache-licensed release (7.10.2) as **OpenSearch** (governed by the Linux Foundation's OpenSearch Software Foundation since 2024), and Elastic added AGPLv3 as an option in 2024. Core search APIs look similar, but clients, plugins and newer features are not interchangeable — choose one deliberately.

sections.title: Cache Invalidation: The Hardest Problem in Caching
sections.content:
Phil Karlton famously said: 'There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.' Cache invalidation is the problem of keeping cached data consistent with the source of truth when the source of truth changes.

**TTL-based invalidation** is the simplest strategy: accept that cached data is stale for up to TTL seconds and set a TTL short enough that the staleness is acceptable. This works well for data that changes infrequently (static content, rarely-updated configuration) or where brief staleness has no business consequence. The risk is always: what if the TTL is too long and a significant data change happens just after the cache is populated?

**Event-driven invalidation** is more precise: whenever a write happens to the database, the application (or a CDC — Change Data Capture — pipeline reading the database's change log) publishes an event that deletes or updates the affected cache keys. This can achieve near-immediate consistency. The challenge is ensuring the invalidation event is reliably sent even when the application crashes mid-write. A common pattern: wrap the database write and the Redis `DEL` in a try block; if the `DEL` fails, the TTL serves as the safety net.

**Cache key namespacing** helps manage bulk invalidation. Instead of invalidating individual keys when a user updates their profile, you can version your cache keys: `user:1001:v3` where the version is stored separately. To invalidate all cache entries for a user, you increment their version — all old cache keys become unreachable (they will expire naturally via TTL) and new reads populate keys with the new version suffix.

**The write-then-invalidate order matters**: you should always **write the database first, then invalidate the cache** — never the reverse. If you invalidate the cache first, a concurrent reader might re-populate the cache with old data from the database before your write completes, creating a stale cache entry that outlives your write. Writing to the database first and then deleting the cache key means the usual worst case is a brief window where the cache holds old data until the delete completes.

One rarer race remains even in this order: a reader misses the cache and reads the *old* row, the writer then updates the database and deletes the key, and only afterwards does the slow reader `SET` its old value into the cache — stale until the TTL expires. This is why the TTL safety net is never optional. Stricter fixes include a second, delayed delete a second or so after the write, version checks on cache writes, or lease tokens (as in Facebook's memcache) that invalidate in-flight fills.

**Interview and production traps to know cold:**

**Never cache unbounded data**: if a cache key holds a list that could grow to millions of items, you are not caching — you are creating a memory leak. Cache aggregate results (counts, pre-paginated slices) rather than full datasets.

**Avoid 'cache poisoning'**: if a failed database query result (an error or empty result) is cached, all subsequent requests will also get the error until TTL expires. Cache `null` or empty results intentionally with a short TTL to avoid hammering the database on a sustained error condition, but track the distinction between 'this user has no items' (valid, cacheable) and 'the database is down' (error, do not cache).

**Redis is not a lock service**: distributed locks via `SET NX EX` work for simple cases but are not fully safe under network partitions (look up the Redlock controversy). A paused or slow lock holder can keep working after its lock expired; protecting the resource requires **fencing tokens** (a monotonically increasing number the storage layer checks), which Redis locks do not provide. For critical distributed locking, use a consensus-based coordination service (etcd, ZooKeeper), or treat Redis locks as an efficiency optimisation (avoiding duplicate work), not a correctness guarantee.

**Elasticsearch is eventually consistent for indexing**: a document is not searchable the instant you index it — the default 1-second refresh interval means there is a small window where the document exists in the datastore but is not yet in the inverted index. If your application immediately queries Elasticsearch after indexing, you may not see the result. If a request must read its own write, index with `refresh=wait_for` (waits for the next scheduled refresh). Avoid `refresh=true` (forces an immediate refresh, creating many tiny segments) outside tests — in production it kills throughput.

items: **Redis** is an in-memory data store with sub-millisecond latency. Its six core data types — strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams — each map to specific use cases; choosing the right type is as important as using Redis at all.

**Redis executes commands on one thread** (I/O threads since 6.0 only handle networking), so each command, MULTI/EXEC block and Lua script is atomic — and one slow command blocks everyone. Persistence is optional: RDB snapshots and/or AOF (`everysec` ≈ 1 s of loss); replication is async, so failover can drop acknowledged writes.

**TTL** is the fundamental mechanism for bounding cache staleness. Set it short enough that stale data does not cause business issues, and combine it with active invalidation (deleting the key on writes) for near-immediate consistency.

**Eviction policies** govern what Redis removes when `maxmemory` is reached. Use `allkeys-lru` for a pure cache, `volatile-lru` for mixed cache+store, and `allkeys-lfu` when access patterns have strong hot/cold skew.

**Cache stampede** occurs when a popular key expires and many concurrent requests flood the database simultaneously. Mitigate with a mutex/lease on refill (`SET NX EX`), request coalescing, TTL jitter, probabilistic early expiration, or serving stale while refreshing in the background.

**Inverted indexes** map every term in a document corpus to a posting list of document IDs. Full-text search engines look up query terms, intersect posting lists, and rank results using BM25, which balances term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalisation.

**Cache invalidation order** matters: write the database first, then delete the cache key. Deleting first lets a concurrent reader re-cache old data; even the right order has a rare slow-reader race, so always keep a TTL as the safety net.

**Elasticsearch/OpenSearch** are not a replacement for a relational database — no ACID transactions, and documents become searchable only after a refresh (~1 s by default; durability comes from the translog). For modest scale, PostgreSQL full-text search (`tsvector` + GIN) avoids running a second system.

**Licensing (2024–25)**: Redis went source-available in 2024 (Valkey forked under BSD), then added AGPLv3 in Redis 8; Elasticsearch went SSPL/ELv2 in 2021 (OpenSearch forked), then added AGPLv3 in 2024. Forks are compatible for basics but diverging.

quiz.question: Which Redis data type is best suited for implementing a leaderboard where users must be retrieved in descending score order?
options: List — because it supports ordered push and pop
Hash — because it stores field-value pairs efficiently
Set — because it supports union and intersection operations
Sorted Set — because each member has a score and ZREVRANGE returns members by descending score
quiz.explanation: Redis Sorted Sets (ZSETs) assign each member a float score and maintain members in sorted order. ZREVRANGE (or ZRANGE ... REV on Redis 6.2+) returns members from highest to lowest score in O(log n + k), making them ideal for leaderboards. Lists are ordered by insertion position, not by a numeric score, so they cannot efficiently answer 'give me the top 10 by score'.

quiz.question: Which Redis eviction policy is most appropriate for a pure cache where any key can safely be removed when memory is full?
options: noeviction — it prevents data loss by returning an error
volatile-lru — it evicts the least recently used key among those with a TTL
allkeys-lru — it evicts the least recently used key from all keys
volatile-ttl — it evicts the key with the shortest remaining TTL
quiz.explanation: allkeys-lru evicts the least recently used key across all keys when memory is full, regardless of whether the key has a TTL. This is the standard choice for a pure cache where all data is regenerable. noeviction would cause write failures; volatile-lru only considers keys with TTLs and may refuse to evict if no TTL keys exist; volatile-ttl is a valid alternative but less predictable than LRU.

quiz.question: In the cache-aside pattern, what is the correct sequence of steps on a cache miss?
options: Query the database, write the result to the cache with a TTL, return the result
Write a placeholder to the cache, query the database, update the cache entry
Return an error to the client and queue the request for background processing
Delete all related cache keys, query the database, return the result without caching
quiz.explanation: Cache-aside (lazy loading) works like this on a miss: (1) query the database for the authoritative data, (2) write the result to the cache with a TTL so future requests are served from cache, (3) return the result to the caller. Writing a placeholder first would cause race conditions; returning an error is wrong because the database is the fallback; skipping the cache write defeats the purpose of caching.

quiz.question: What is a cache stampede, and what is its primary cause?
options: Redis running out of memory and evicting keys faster than they can be repopulated
Many concurrent requests hitting the database simultaneously when a popular cached key expires
A misconfigured TTL causing the cache to serve stale data indefinitely
Multiple Redis instances returning inconsistent data due to replication lag
quiz.explanation: A cache stampede (thundering herd) occurs when a popular key expires in the cache and many concurrent requests, all finding the cache empty at the same time, simultaneously fall through to the database. The database receives a sudden spike in load that can cause degradation or failure. Solutions include distributed locks, probabilistic early expiration, and background refresh.

quiz.question: What does an inverted index map each token to?
options: A posting list of document IDs where that token appears
The position of the token within a single document
The full content of the document containing that token
The BM25 relevance score for that token across the corpus
quiz.explanation: An inverted index maps each unique token (normalised word) to a posting list — an ordered list of document IDs that contain that token. At query time, the search engine looks up each query term in this index and intersects or unions the posting lists to find matching documents. The inverted index does not store full document content or pre-computed scores — scoring is computed at query time.

quiz.question: Why does `LIKE '%keyword%'` with a leading wildcard perform poorly on large tables?
options: LIKE does not support case-insensitive matching
A leading wildcard prevents the database from using a B+ tree index, forcing a full table scan
LIKE returns results in random order with no relevance ranking
LIKE is limited to VARCHAR columns and cannot search TEXT fields
quiz.explanation: A B+ tree index stores values in sorted order, so the database can use it to quickly find rows where a column starts with a known prefix. A leading wildcard ('%keyword') means the matching portion can start anywhere in the string — the index cannot narrow the search and must be bypassed. This forces a sequential scan of every row, which is O(n) in table size. Full-text indexes (inverted indexes) are specifically designed to avoid this problem.

quiz.question: In BM25 relevance scoring, what does Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) measure?
options: How many times a term appears in a specific document
How short the document is relative to the average document length in the corpus
How many shards the search was distributed across
How rare a term is across the entire document corpus
quiz.explanation: IDF measures how rare or distinctive a term is across the entire corpus. A term that appears in 90% of documents (like 'the' or 'product') has very low IDF and contributes little to ranking. A term that appears in 0.01% of documents is highly distinctive and receives a high IDF weight, boosting documents that contain it. BM25 multiplies TF by IDF to produce a score that balances frequency within a document against rarity across the corpus.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of operations when updating cached data to avoid a race condition?
options: Delete the cache key first, then write to the database
Write to the database first, then delete or update the cache key
Write to the cache first, then write to the database asynchronously
Write to both the cache and database simultaneously in a single transaction
quiz.explanation: You must write to the database first, then invalidate the cache. If you delete the cache key first, a concurrent reader can re-populate the cache with stale data from the database before your write completes — that stale entry will then persist until its TTL expires. Writing to the database first ensures that any reader who misses the cache after your invalidation reads the new value. (A rare race with a slow reader that fetched the old row before your write still exists, which is why a TTL safety net is always kept.)

quiz.question: Which Redis command pattern implements a distributed lock atomically, preventing a race window between checking existence and setting the key?
options: SETNX key value followed immediately by EXPIRE key ttl
GET key; if nil then SET key value EX ttl
SET key value NX EX ttl
HSET key lock true then EXPIRE key ttl
quiz.explanation: SET key value NX EX ttl is a single atomic command: NX means 'only set if the key does not exist', and EX sets the expiry in seconds. The atomicity is critical — the old two-command pattern (SETNX + EXPIRE) had a race window where the process could crash between the two commands, leaving a lock with no expiry that would never be released. The single SET NX EX command eliminates that window.

quiz.question: What does the Elasticsearch `refresh_interval` setting control, and what is its production implication?
options: The delay between indexing a document and it becoming searchable; default is 1 second
How frequently shard replicas are synchronised; lower values increase replication lag
How often Elasticsearch syncs data to disk; setting it low risks data loss on crash
How often cluster health checks run; setting it high can cause split-brain scenarios
quiz.explanation: The refresh_interval controls how often Elasticsearch writes the in-memory indexing buffer out as a new Lucene segment, making newly indexed documents searchable (durability is handled separately by the translog). The default is 1 second — meaning there is up to a 1-second window where a document has been indexed but is not yet returnable in search results. This 'near real-time' guarantee is a key operational characteristic of Elasticsearch. Setting refresh_interval to -1 during bulk indexing dramatically improves throughput by deferring this flush, at the cost of documents being unsearchable until a manual refresh.
